steps.title: The Prädikat
steps.body: German Prädikatswein is graded by grape sugar at harvest, measured in Oechsle: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, BA, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese, TBA. The levels show ripeness, not the wine's final sweetness. In the Mosel, Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese are often made off-dry or sweet, by tradition.

steps.title: Sweetness terms
steps.body: Trocken means dry, up to 9 g/l of sugar; halbtrocken, off-dry, up to 18 g/l; feinherb, an unofficial off-dry term. Without these words, a Mosel Prädikat wine is usually fruity-sweet, fruchtsüss. The high acidity, often 8 to 10 g/l, balances the sugar, so even sweet wines taste fresh.

steps.prompt: Order the Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Each level demands riper grapes at harvest.

steps.title: Sweet wines
steps.body: In great years, the Mosel makes Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein, from botrytised or frozen grapes, with intense sweetness and acidity. Auctions, like the Grosser Ring auction in Trier, sell rare sweet wines for high prices. These wines age for decades.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prädikat levels show ripeness, from Kabinett to TBA
Trocken means dry; without it, Mosel Prädikats are often sweet
